analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to get opt-in consent before collecting or sharing sensitive personal data, with federal and state enforcement.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: after its introduction and referral in March 2021, it sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2023, despite 29 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring companies to get explicit opt-in consent before collecting, selling, or sharing sensitive personal information such as health records, precise location, browsing history, private messages, and biometric data. Companies would have to publish plain-language privacy policies, let people opt out of sharing nonsensitive data, and pass an independent privacy audit every two years. Enforcement would rest with the FTC and state attorneys general, backed by 500 new FTC hires and $350 million in funding.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users would gain real control over sensitive data: companies could not sell or share their health information, precise location, browsing history, or private messages without explicit consent, and would have to explain in plain language what they collect and with whom they share it. People would also gain the right to opt out of sharing other data at any time, and companies handling sensitive data would face independent audits every two years with results disclosed publicly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of apps, websites, and services

how_it_helps.text: Companies would need affirmative, express, opt-in consent before collecting, transmitting, selling, sharing, or otherwise using sensitive personal information, including sharing it with third parties beyond what was disclosed.

Companies would have to maintain a free, concise, plain-language privacy and data use policy that identifies who is collecting the data, why, which categories of third parties receive it, and how to withdraw consent or access the data.

For nonsensitive personal information, users could opt out of collection, sharing, and sale at any time, and companies would have to pass opt-out requests along to any third parties they shared data with.

Any company handling sensitive data would have to obtain an independent privacy audit at least every two years and publicly disclose whether the audit found it compliant, with audits also provided to the FTC and state attorneys general on request.

The FTC would gain 500 new privacy and data security employees, $350 million in authorized funding, and the power to enforce against common carriers such as phone companies, and state attorneys general could sue violators.

Covered data includes health information, genetic data, precise location, web browsing and app usage history, biometric identifiers, contents of personal communications, immigration status, sexual orientation, and religious beliefs.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect, process, or monetize personal data — social media platforms, apps, data brokers, advertisers, and phone companies — would bear consent, compliance, and biennial audit costs, and some data-driven business models would lose access to sensitive data they currently use without asking.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data-collection companies, platforms, and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The bill contains a national standard that would bar states from adopting or enforcing their own data privacy laws, preserving only state rules on breach notification, biometrics, and wiretapping — so it would override stronger state privacy laws, such as California's, with a single federal floor.

Individuals could not sue to enforce their rights; enforcement is left entirely to the FTC and state attorneys general, and the FTC must give companies 30 days to cure non-willful violations before acting.

The bill exempts large categories of data handling: fraud prevention, completing transactions, loyalty programs, internal product research, marketing with an opt-out, publicly available information, and de-identified data, and employee and job-applicant data is excluded from the definition of sensitive information.
The audit requirement does not apply to companies handling sensitive data on 250,000 or fewer individuals per year, so many small and mid-sized firms would face no independent review.
The FTC would have up to 18 months to write the regulations after enactment, with an additional 180-day effective date, delaying any real protection until roughly two years after passage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would create a genuine national baseline — opt-in consent for sensitive data, readable privacy policies, opt-out rights, and audits — that consumers today largely lack. But its costs to the public's interests are real: it would preempt stronger state privacy laws, give individuals no right to sue on their own, and carve out enough exemptions that consumer advocates viewed it as weaker than the state laws it would displace. It was a compromise bill, and it is fair to say the compromise leaned toward keeping enforcement slow and company-friendly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its consumer protection subcommittee in March 2021, and it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Suzan DelBene introduced the bill on March 11, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
One day later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce, where the action history ends.
The bill drew 29 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action of any kind before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that collect and sell personal data avoided a federal compliance regime and kept the pre-enactment status quo, while consumers gained nothing — though stronger state privacy laws were also left intact, since the bill's preemption provision never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data-collection companies kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 29 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican ever joined, but because the bill never reached a vote, no roll-call ever measured party support directly.

industries.industry: Big tech platforms and the adtech/data-broker ecosystem
industries.note: The bill would have imposed opt-in consent, plain-language disclosure, and biennial audits on platforms and data brokers, cutting off some sensitive-data uses they profit from today. But the same bill would have given these companies a single uniform national standard that wipes out stronger state privacy laws and leaves individuals unable to sue — an outcome industry had sought.

industries.industry: Data brokers and targeted advertising firms
industries.note: Selling or sharing sensitive data such as health information, precise location, and browsing history would require explicit opt-in consent, which would shrink markets built on quietly trading this data. Here the industry's cost is the public's gain.

The mandatory two-year audit requirement would create a recurring market for independent auditors, and the bill directs the FTC to write rules keeping auditors from selling remedies under cover of the audit.

Common carriers, normally outside FTC authority, would be newly covered, subjecting their data practices to federal privacy rules for the first time. The cost of compliance comes with clearer, uniform rules.
